# Test suites that CI runs in the `integration` job, against a real Postgres.
#
# These are the second half of #7. Every suite below was measured twice, once
# against the unroutable placeholder the `static` job uses and once against a
# real PostgreSQL 16: each one FAILS without a database and PASSES with one.
# That is the whole entry requirement, and it is why they cannot live in
# `static` and could never have passed there.
#
# To re-verify this list, or to check a suite before adding one:
#
#   # must FAIL
#   DATABASE_URL=postgresql://ci:ci@127.0.0.1:1/unused \
#   TEST_DATABASE_URL=$DATABASE_URL DIRECT_URL=$DATABASE_URL \
#   JWT_SECRET=ci-not-a-real-secret npx jest --runTestsByPath <path> --ci
#
#   # must PASS
#   DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/backenly_test \
#   TEST_DATABASE_URL=$DATABASE_URL DIRECT_URL=$DATABASE_URL \
#   JWT_SECRET=ci-not-a-real-secret npx jest --runTestsByPath <path> --ci
#
# A suite that passes BOTH ways belongs in database-free-suites.txt instead —
# putting it here would burn a Postgres service container to prove nothing.
#
# Suites that fail even WITH a database are deliberately not here. They are
# listed, with the measured reason, in suites-not-in-ci.txt. Adding a known-red
# suite to a blocking job is how CI became permanently red before (see the note
# on `tests/core` in ci.yml); a red that is always red carries no information.

__tests__/billing/purchased-credits-extend-the-cap.test.ts

__tests__/retry-logic.test.ts

# Connect auto-wiring does what its receipt lists: Stripe adds the payment
# columns and registers a webhook handler in the one shape the receiver fires,
# email providers wire the on_signup welcome trigger only where auth exists,
# and every connect syncs activeIntegrations. The live provider probe and the
# LLM generator are the two stubbed seams; vault, executor and DDL are real.
tests/integration/integrations-autowiring.spec.ts
# Realtime surfaces CI can honestly cover: SSE tickets burn in the project's
# real _token_blacklist ledger (single-use, expiry, project binding) and the
# broadcast route enforces its payload cap over a real pg_notify. Frame
# delivery through the LISTEN hub stays a staging case.
tests/integration/realtime-ticket-broadcast.spec.ts
tests/integration/export-database-rls.spec.ts
tests/integration/postgres-admin.spec.ts

# Needs a real Postgres AND a git worktree of an older release.
#
# It builds a genuine old install from that release's own schema.prisma rather
# than downgrading the current one, because a hand-made artefact would prove
# nothing about what operators actually have on disk. It also creates and drops
# throwaway databases, so it needs CREATEDB.
tests/integration/selfhost-upgrade.spec.ts

# Needs a real Postgres, and a real Redis for the limiter half.
#
# It severs the database at the TRANSPORT through a proxy rather than stopping
# the server, because the only Postgres on a developer's machine is the one
# their work depends on - and what the pool experiences is identical either way.
# A genuine server restart is the self-host CI job's business, where a real
# deployment exists.
tests/integration/restart-recovery.spec.ts

# Needs REDIS, not Postgres.
#
# The `integration` job is where CI runs suites that require a real backing
# service, and this one requires a different service from the rest. It holds to
# the same rule they do: it FAILS without its dependency rather than skipping,
# so it can never sit green having tested nothing. Verify it the same way,
# with and without REDIS_URL rather than with and without a database.
tests/integration/rate-limit-shared-store.spec.ts

# The ProjectResolver regression matrix (commit 2). Pins the behaviour the ~70
# authorization call sites are being migrated TO, before they are migrated, so
# the migration cannot quietly redefine it. Measured the same way as everything
# above: fails against the unroutable placeholder, passes against a real
# PostgreSQL. Every assertion lives in a `where` clause, which is exactly what a
# mocked client cannot model.
__tests__/auth/project-resolver.test.ts

# The tenant-isolation adapter (commit 2b). withTenantIsolation -> requireProjectId
# -> getCurrentProjectId is now the single decision point for 36 route files, so
# its contract is pinned directly and then again through a real route. Needs a
# database and real signed sessions: the defect lived in a `where` clause and an
# auth branch, neither of which a mocked client models.
__tests__/auth/tenant-isolation-adapter.test.ts

# Representative authorization matrix for app/api/projects/[id]/** (commit 2c).
# One route per authentication pattern rather than 35 near-identical tests,
# because the authorization decision is now identical across the family and only
# the plumbing differs. Asserts the 404-for-both behaviour is preserved, so
# migrating authorization did not start leaking project existence.
__tests__/auth/project-routes-authorization.test.ts

# Project deletion (commit 2c-2b). The only destructive operation the
# authorization migration WIDENS: DELETE /api/projects/[id] was owner-only and
# is now reachable by an organization ADMIN. It drops every workspace schema the
# project owns and there is no undo, so the VIEWER/DEVELOPER/ADMIN/OWNER matrix
# gets its own suite rather than being folded into the general route tests.
__tests__/auth/project-delete-authorization.test.ts

# Workspace OAuth client credentials (end-user social sign-in). The routes took
# the project from the x-project-id header after requireAuth and nothing else,
# so any signed-in account could list, replace or delete another project's OAuth
# client. Pins the role ladder: stranger nothing (404, no existence oracle),
# VIEWER read, DEVELOPER save, ADMIN delete. Real sessions, real resolver, real
# membership rows.
__tests__/auth/workspace-oauth-authorization.test.ts

# The workspace ZIP download had the same shape: authenticated, then the header
# project id trusted. Pins that the guard is getCurrentProjectId like its
# workspace/files siblings: 401 / 403 / 404 / 400 before any disk access, and an
# authorized caller reaches the route's own disk lookup.
__tests__/auth/workspace-download-authorization.test.ts

# The catalog routes (schemas, indexes, relationships) read only the named
# project's own schemas, from its own database: a second tenant's schema,
# real and populated beside the first, is never listed and is refused 403 when
# named; the platform view is refused; the project's own answers are real.
__tests__/auth/catalog-routes-own-schema.test.ts

# Next's own /api/v1/{projectId} routes (end-user auth, healthz, and every route
# recordedV1 wraps) answer a locked or paused project with the runtime gate's
# 503, codes and words, and reach their handlers again once it serves.
tests/integration/next-routes-serving-gate.spec.ts

# Credential surfaces are held to a role, not to membership. The Connect page's
# routes (mint/revoke MCP keys, read/provision/rotate direct Postgres
# credentials, full pg_dump export) authorized with withProjectValidation alone,
# so a Cloud organization VIEWER could mint a full-write mcp_live_ key or
# exfiltrate the tenant. Pins the floor: VIEWER/DEVELOPER 403 with no side
# effect, ADMIN/OWNER allowed, masked key list stays a VIEWER read, and
# single-tenant operators unaffected. Real sessions, resolver and guard.
__tests__/auth/connect-credential-authorization.test.ts

# Provider secrets: the platform AuthProvider collection is admin-only and
# redacted, and per-project deploy-provider credentials are ADMIN-floored with
# the decrypted material never leaving the server (INT-11 / INT-12).
tests/integration/provider-credential-floors.spec.ts
# Settings API keys are a PROJECT surface (admins see and revoke agent keys,
# ex-members do not), and the withProjectAccess routes carry explicit floors:
# share-report ADMIN, Supabase import DEVELOPER (SET-03 / SET-04).
tests/integration/settings-keys-and-floors.spec.ts

# Operate decisions (approve a parked agent request, run or undo a repair,
# dismiss findings, set the autonomy dial, grant Tier-2 maintenance consent,
# create/merge/discard branches, publish) authorized membership only, so a Cloud
# VIEWER could be the "human approval" the safety model hinges on. Pins the
# floors: DEVELOPER for build-grade decisions, ADMIN for approvals, consent,
# merge and rollback; reads stay VIEWER; single-tenant operators unaffected.
__tests__/auth/operate-role-floors.test.ts
# Blocking an end user must flip the row. The workspace users table is FORCE
# row-level security, and BLOCK_USER/UNBLOCK_USER ran their UPDATE with no
# claims, so under the production app role every approved block answered "not
# found" and changed nothing. Pins the FORCE premise under a non-superuser
# role, that the executor takes the service-role claims path, and the real
# row flip both ways through the real executor door.
__tests__/auth/block-user-rls.test.ts
# A blocked end user's token is refused at request time under the app role.
# The runtime's resolver and Next's v1 middleware read users.is_blocked with no
# claims, which FORCE row-level security answers with no row for a
# non-bypassing role, so the token was accepted. Pins the premise and both
# checks with the project's client running as such a role.
__tests__/auth/blocked-token-under-app-role.test.ts
# Every other path that takes or issues an end-user token applies revocation
# and blocking, under the same non-bypassing role: Next's v1 middleware reads a
# token in Authorization as the runtime does, the storage download and
# accept-invite resolve theirs through the shared check (accept-invite reading
# the email as the service role), OAuth, magic-link and reset sign-ins refuse a
# blocked user and still sign the others in, and the function runner gives a
# revoked or blocked token no identity. Real users, link and teams tables, and
# the real flows, are the property.
__tests__/auth/end-user-token-paths.test.ts
# ENABLE_REALTIME answered "Realtime active" for tables that never streamed: a
# failed CREATE TRIGGER (missing/wrong-case table) was a footnote under the
# banner, a refused table (internal, auth-managed users) was listed under
# "Enabled by this call", and an empty project got "active for 0 table(s)".
# Pins failure codes, refusal reasons, catalog read-back gating, the skipped
# ledger on project-wide calls, and the honest empty-project answer.
__tests__/services/realtime-enable-honesty.test.ts
# The dashboard's Insert/Edit/Delete row buttons ran bare prisma writes, which
# FORCE row-level security refuses under the production app role — the better
# the agent's RLS, the more broken the data grid. getTableRows was fixed to
# read as owner; the writes were not. Pins the refusal premise under a
# non-superuser role, all three writes through the service-role machinery
# (environment-independent mechanism pin), and the real row effects.
__tests__/database/dashboard-row-writes-rls.test.ts

# A realtime change reaches a subscriber only if that subscriber could select
# the row: a real own-rows policy, two end users, anonymous and service-role
# subscribers, deletes reduced to the key, and a table without a primary key.
__tests__/database/realtime-row-visibility.test.ts
# Schema snapshots stored ZERO tables (the parser expected a format the
# introspector never emitted), so the History snapshot view was always empty
# and rollback diffed two empty sets and reported "Dropped 0 table(s)" as
# success. Pins catalog-true snapshots (columns, types, uniques, defaults,
# FKs), a real rollback that names what it dropped, the users-table guard,
# honest failure when dropped structure cannot be recreated, and the no-diff
# answer.
__tests__/database/schema-version-snapshots.test.ts

# Monitoring read what nothing writes: metrics/errors read the Log table (its
# only writers are platform auth events with no projectId) and told every
# project "No API metrics available yet" / "Your APIs are running smoothly"
# while api_request_logs held the traffic and the 500s; the Logs tab was empty
# forever. Pins metrics/errors derived from the runtime record (branch rows
# excluded, windows honoured, session-timezone-proof bounds) and the explorer
# serving the union of both stores with working filters and DB-side counts.
__tests__/monitoring/monitoring-truth.test.ts

# Trigger webhooks fired a RAW fetch on the stored URL from the web process and
# persisted the failure text — an SSRF primitive with a persistence layer,
# readable back over MCP — while endpoint webhooks had already moved to
# safeFetch. And syncWebhookCapture's "after a table is added" contract had no
# caller on any creation path, so webhooks never saw rows in newer tables.
# Pins guard-validated creation, guarded delivery (raw fetch never touched),
# the capped stored failure, and the capture sync on CREATE_TABLE.
__tests__/services/trigger-webhook-egress.test.ts
# ApiKey.permissions was written by set_key_permissions and the key editor but
# never read by the data plane: /api/v1 db and /api/v2 served writes to any
# valid key, so narrowing a leaked key to ['read'] changed nothing while the
# tool answered "permissions updated". Pins the method gate on BOTH doors
# (read-only refused on writes with INSUFFICIENT_KEY_PERMISSIONS, read+write
# and service-role unaffected) and that SET_KEY_PERMISSIONS over the real
# executor takes effect on the very next request. Real server, real socket.
tests/integration/key-permission-gate.spec.ts
# A parked branch merge replayed the migration log as it was at EXECUTION time,
# so an agent could park an innocent merge and append statements before the
# human clicked approve — breaking the approvals contract "what executes is
# exactly what the human read". Pins the approved statement list frozen into
# the request: a grown log refuses MERGE_STALE (unit and end-to-end through
# createApprovalRequest/decideApproval), a matching log merges, and the
# console's unpinned live-diff merge is unchanged.
__tests__/branches/merge-approval-freeze.test.ts

# Single-tenant bootstrap (commit 3). Runs the real script against a database it
# creates and drops, because everything worth asserting is a side effect on
# Postgres: a schema that exists, a row that was not duplicated, a refusal that
# happened before anything was written. It cannot share this job's database:
# bootstrap counts projects globally and the shared one holds many, which is
# itself asserted as the incompatible-database case.
__tests__/bootstrap/single-tenant-bootstrap.test.ts

# The self-hosted single-account claim (commit 3 follow-up). The pre-flight
# check in assertSignupAllowed runs ~50 lines before the insert, so it cannot be
# the enforcement: two concurrent first signups would both read zero accounts.
# The claim is made inside the inserting transaction behind an advisory lock,
# and this asserts it under genuine concurrency rather than in sequence.
__tests__/auth/first-account-claim.test.ts

# setup-postgrest-roles idempotency (commit 3 follow-up). --apply used to run
# ALTER ROLE ... PASSWORD unconditionally with a fresh random password, so
# re-running a command documented as repeatable rotated the credential a live
# PostgREST authenticates with. Roles are CLUSTER-WIDE, so this suite uses a
# throwaway authenticator and its own database.
__tests__/bootstrap/postgrest-roles-idempotency.test.ts

# Single-tenant ownership: THE project is created before anyone signs up, so it
# starts owner-less and must adopt the first operator. Runs the real script
# against its own database, because the failure was a state the database was
# allowed to sit in.
__tests__/bootstrap/single-tenant-ownership.test.ts

# What a new self-hoster READS on the documented first run. That run exits 3 by
# design, but it used to open with raw Prisma error blocks, because bootstrap
# discovered its optional superuser helpers were missing by calling them and
# catching the failure - and Prisma logs a failed query at `error` level before
# any catch runs. Asserts the OUTPUT, since the exit code was always correct.
# Needs its own database: the text depends on the helpers being genuinely
# absent, which is not true of the shared one.
__tests__/bootstrap/install-path-output.test.ts

# First self-hosted operator admission. Needs a user table with ZERO rows, which
# a shared database cannot guarantee, so it runs against its own.
__tests__/auth/first-operator-admission.test.ts

# ProjectLifecycle, the Phase 7 edition seam for "which projects exist, and may
# another be created". Every assertion is a property of rows: that single-tenant
# resolves THE pinned project while a second row sits in the same table, that
# its refusal happens BEFORE the insert, and that Cloud creation provisions a
# graph, a workspace, a schema and a signing secret rather than one row.
__tests__/edition/project-lifecycle.test.ts

# FleetScheduler, the Phase 7 edition seam for "which projects does a scheduled
# pass run against". The property under test is a `where` clause: single-tenant
# must return THE project while a second, equally eligible row sits in the same
# table. A mock cannot show that, and "returns one project" would pass against
# an enumeration that happened to find one.
__tests__/edition/fleet-scheduler.test.ts

# The migration-lineage probe, against a real engine. Four properties have no
# meaning without one: that a whole migration file survives as a single
# submission (Prisma's raw API cannot send one at all), that the capture reads
# the semantics the comparison depends on rather than object names, that the RLS
# reads see a policy that exists, and that a scratch database is always dropped.
tests/integration/migration-lineage-probe-db.spec.ts

# The canonical migration chain against a real engine. Once a forward migration
# exists, "the baseline equals schema.prisma" is no longer the invariant and is
# no longer checkable statically: the live property is that baseline plus every
# migration after it equals the model, and only Prisma can answer it, by
# replaying the chain into a shadow database. This is the gate that catches a
# schema.prisma edit shipped without a migration.
tests/integration/managed-db-canonical-history.spec.ts

# The Phase 6b primitives against a real engine. The executor's governance is
# decided in TypeScript and is unit tested; these three primitives generate SQL,
# and nothing about whether that SQL is correct can be learned without
# PostgreSQL running it. It earned the slot immediately: the first run found
# that the backfill cursor used max(k), and PostgreSQL has no max() aggregate
# for uuid — the most common primary key on this platform.
tests/integration/maintenance-phase6b.spec.ts

# Resolving a plan that was never stored. Every step is a database read: the
# finding, the subsystem clustering, the structural diagnosis and the catalog
# fingerprint. It also documents what a project must actually look like before
# a dry run can return anything but WOULD_REFUSE — 50+ analysed rows, and
# exactly one live hypothesis rather than a tie the diagnosis will not break.
tests/integration/maintenance-resolve-db.spec.ts

# The maintenance primitives against a table the PRODUCT built, which means one
# with row-level security on it. Every other fixture here uses raw DDL and so
# has no RLS, which is exactly why reconcile.ts could read zero rows from a
# table holding eighty and call it "no rows" — for months, with every suite
# green. It also creates a throwaway NOSUPERUSER role, because the local
# development role is a superuser and superusers bypass RLS entirely, so a
# superuser-only test would prove nothing about production.
tests/integration/maintenance-rls-aware.spec.ts

# Restore must never destroy a project and report success. It did: DROP plus
# CREATE, then a dump whose own first statement is CREATE SCHEMA, an aborted
# --single-transaction restore, and psql exiting 0 because ON_ERROR_STOP was
# unset. Observed as 3 tables and 5 rows before, 0 tables after, success:true.
# Needs a real database, a real pg_dump and a real psql: the defect lived in
# the interaction between the dump's contents and psql's exit code, so any
# mock would have tested the mock.
__tests__/services/backup-restore-integrity.test.ts

# Backup and restore under a PRODUCTION-style role rather than a superuser.
# Every other test of this path runs as the local development role, which is a
# superuser, and superusers bypass RLS — so a superuser-only test proves
# nothing about the deployment that matters. That gap hid a four-day production
# backup outage. This builds a NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS application role owning
# FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY tables, plus a dedicated BYPASSRLS backup role with
# CONNECT, USAGE and SELECT and nothing else, and asserts the minimal privilege
# contract the README documents. Needs CREATE ROLE, so it is database-backed.
__tests__/services/backup-restore-privileges.test.ts

# The table editor's constraint picker. The foreign-key executor INFERS a target
# when none is given, which is right for the AI path and wrong for a picker: an
# operator's explicit choice was being discarded in favour of a guess. The
# fixture makes inference and the choice DISAGREE, and asserts on the catalog
# rather than on what the executor reported.
__tests__/database/constraint-picker.test.ts

# The logs explorer's query. /api/logs answered "how many, and how many of each
# severity" by loading every matching row into memory for a .length and four
# .filter().length calls, then discarding them - a full table read per request
# on a page whose search box fires on every change. Nothing caught it because
# the ANSWERS were right, so this pins the answers AND the tenant scoping, with
# a second project holding more rows of every severity.
__tests__/database/logs-explorer-query.test.ts

# The credential split. The application used to connect as POSTGRES_USER, which
# initdb creates as a SUPERUSER - and superusers bypass RLS, including FORCE
# ROW LEVEL SECURITY, so every policy the platform wrote was advisory for the
# application itself. Runs the real script, then reconnects as the role it made
# and watches the database refuse. A contrast test shows the superuser still
# sees every row, so the isolation assertion cannot pass vacuously.
__tests__/database/app-role-separation.test.ts

# Claiming a self-hosted deployment. The installer said "ready" while the
# project had no owner, so the first account could not use the dashboard until
# somebody ran bootstrap a second time. Signup now binds the administrator to
# the project in one transaction, gated on a token the installer prints -
# possession of the machine grants the claim rather than whoever loads the page
# first. Covers the race, the replay, and adoption itself.
__tests__/auth/deployment-claim.test.ts

# Emailed six-digit codes for platform signup and password reset. The code is
# only safe short because it can be guessed a few times, online, and used once:
# the attempt budget is one conditional UPDATE and single use is one conditional
# DELETE, so both are asserted under real concurrency against Postgres.
#
# The routes suite drives signup and reset end to end against a real STARTTLS
# SMTP sink, reading each code out of the mail that actually arrived, and
# includes the production failure where the provider rejected the sending
# domain while every page still said "sent".
__tests__/auth/email-code.test.ts
__tests__/auth/email-code-routes.test.ts

# Signing out ends this browser's sessions from any state: live, access expired
# with a live refresh cookie, cookie-only, Bearer and cookie drifted apart, or
# already signed out. It ends only what the request presents, refuses
# cross-site browser requests, and logout-all still needs a live session. The
# refresh route is driven afterwards to prove the token cannot be replayed.
# Fails 12/12 without a database, passes 12/12 with one.
__tests__/auth/session-lifecycle-routes.test.ts

# An OAuth sign-in carries no setup token, so it must not be able to claim a
# self-hosted deployment - and the Google and GitHub callbacks used to create
# the first account without asking. Needs a users table with ZERO rows, which a
# shared database cannot guarantee, so it runs against a database of its own.
__tests__/auth/oauth-claim-gate.test.ts

# The read-only SQL workspace. /api/database/query used to run queryRaw on the
# APPLICATION connection with a deny-list regex as its only tenant boundary -
# and before the credential split that connection was a superuser. Its sibling
# /api/cli/query was moved onto the governed bkn_ro_ engine in July for exactly
# that reason; this route was left behind, with no callers and no tests. The
# suite bypasses the parser deliberately and asserts POSTGRES refuses, with
# positive reads present so the refusals cannot pass because nothing works.
__tests__/database/sql-workspace-isolation.test.ts

# Function SQL ran on the app's own connection, whose role owns every platform
# table and workspace schema, so generated function code could read public.users
# or another tenant's tables; claims filter rows, not schemas. It now logs in as
# the project's own role. The suite runs the real runner and asserts POSTGRES
# refuses, including after RESET ROLE, with positive reads and writes present
# so the refusals cannot pass because nothing works.
__tests__/database/function-sql-isolation.test.ts

# Cross-tenant schema history. The route called verifyToken and stopped, so any
# authenticated account could read another tenant's schema snapshots and roll
# back their schema. Underneath, getSchemaVersion looked up by version id alone
# and stripped projectId from its result, so no caller could have checked even
# if it tried - and rollbackToVersion used it. Tested at the library boundary,
# because scoping the query is what makes the bug unrepresentable.
__tests__/auth/schema-version-isolation.test.ts

# The ai-workspace routes took projectId from the request body and used it
# unchecked, so any signed-in account could name another tenant's project and
# apply schema changes to it. Two-sided: every denial is paired with the
# corresponding permission, because a refusal-only suite is green when nothing
# works. Runs as CLOUD, since single-tenant treats any authenticated account as
# the deployment's operator and the question does not arise there.
__tests__/auth/ai-workspace-tenant-isolation.test.ts

# PUT /api/users/[userId] discarded requireAuth's result and applied the body to
# where: { id: params.userId }. The body accepts password, roleId, emailVerified
# and twoFactorEnabled, so one authenticated request was account takeover,
# privilege escalation and 2FA bypass. Separates WHO may touch a record from
# WHICH fields they may set: self-service must not become self-promotion.
__tests__/auth/user-record-authorization.test.ts

# DELETE on the same route checked only that the caller was signed in, so any
# account could delete any other with every project it owned. Admin only now,
# and not self-service (that is /api/auth/delete-account). Calls the real
# handler; two-sided.
__tests__/auth/user-delete-authorization.test.ts
# A fresh install must not fill its log with errors about a non-event. The
# autonomy sweep purges end-user auth tables that do not exist until a project
# enables auth; its information_schema pre-check treated an EMPTY answer as a
# failed lookup, which is exactly what a brand-new workspace returns. Observes
# the output from a SUBPROCESS: an in-process capture saw nothing and passed
# identically against the bug.
__tests__/services/fresh-install-auth-purge.test.ts

# Every "fixed" claim comes from a recorded, re-checked outcome: /health says
# how each finding closed and counts only confirmed repairs, POST /health only
# dismisses, the away digest and event feed mark unconfirmed changes as such
# and claim no rollback, and the loop's sensor record names checks that could
# not run. Real findings, audit rows and preferences are the property.
tests/integration/fixed-claims-from-verified-state.spec.ts

# Support cases at the real routes: owner-scoped reads and writes (another
# account's case is 404), the paid-plan severity gate, the status machine
# (reply reopens, closed refuses), the AI first responder recording
# replied/unavailable/failed truthfully, and 404 CLOUD_ONLY_FEATURE off Cloud.
# Case rows, thread rows and the in-app notification are the property.
tests/integration/support-center.spec.ts

# Five destructive routes that did not check who was asking. Three had NO
# authentication at all - anyone reaching the server could roll back a live
# deployment or rebuild a workspace database. Two verified a token and then
# checked the caller's PLAN ENTITLEMENT, which reads like a permission check
# and is not one. Two-sided, and asserts the victim's state is unchanged after
# a denial, because "denied" and "denied and did nothing" are different claims.
__tests__/auth/destructive-route-authorization.test.ts

# Passing a tenant id into a service is not evidence the service uses it.
# getWorkspaceUsers took a projectId, ignored it, and ran an unqualified
# SELECT ... FROM users on the PLATFORM connection - returning every account
# email on the deployment for any projectId. generate-fix had no auth and could
# regenerate a victim's stored sqlFix, the field apply-fix runs through
# $executeRawUnsafe: cross-tenant fix poisoning, not SQL injection. Asserts the
# victim's fix is byte-for-byte unchanged after a denied write.
__tests__/auth/tenant-scoped-service-queries.test.ts

# The deployment recovery bundle, written from a real database. The two things
# most likely to be wrong cannot be seen from the pg_dump arguments alone: that
# the encryption protects anything, and that the dropped tables are actually
# empty in the dump. A known secret is planted and must appear nowhere in the
# bundle bytes AND must appear once opened with the credential - the second half
# is what proves the first half's search would have noticed. A live session is
# planted for the same reason, so "no session rows" cannot pass against a
# database that simply had none.
__tests__/recovery/export-bundle.test.ts

# Recovery onto a machine that has never seen the deployment. The target is a
# database created empty seconds earlier, so nothing can be silently borrowed
# from the environment - which is what makes a restore test run on the source
# machine worthless. Asserts both locked semantics: the project signing secret
# comes back byte-for-byte, the revoked JTI is still revoked, and the planted
# session and magic link are gone while their tables exist and are empty. Each
# has a paired assertion that the source really held the row, so none can pass
# vacuously.
__tests__/recovery/clean-machine-restore.test.ts

# Restoring over a deployment that is already running. The clean-machine case is
# what the product is for; this is the one that can do damage. A marker row is
# written into a live target, a deliberately corrupted bundle and then a wrong
# credential are offered, and the marker must still be there afterwards -
# workspace-backup restored by dropping the schema first and reading the dump
# second, so an unreadable dump destroyed a working schema. Then the good bundle
# must REPLACE rather than merge, because a restore that leaves newer rows
# produces a deployment matching no point in time at all. Run twice, since an
# interrupted restore gets re-run.
__tests__/recovery/destructive-restore.test.ts

# ── Dependency failure ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# Restart qualification asks whether a deployment comes back. These ask what it
# SAYS while a dependency is actually gone, which is a different question and is
# where the dishonest answers live. Each one found a real defect:
#
#   postgres  every authorization wrapper reported a database outage as 401,
#             so a signed-in operator was told their credentials were rejected -
#             and the obvious response, signing out and back in, destroys the
#             session and cannot succeed while the same database is down
#   storage   both drivers collapsed "cannot read the bytes" into null, which
#             both callers render as 404, so an unmounted volume told every
#             caller their objects had ceased to exist
#
# The postgres suite cuts the transport with a proxy rather than stopping the
# server, for the reason tests/helpers/severable-proxy.ts states, and repoints
# DATABASE_URL BEFORE importing the routes so the product's own singleton is
# what loses its database.
tests/integration/dependency-failure-postgres.spec.ts
tests/integration/dependency-failure-storage.spec.ts

# Needs REDIS, not Postgres — same rule as rate-limit-shared-store.spec.ts, so
# verify it with and without REDIS_URL rather than with and without a database.
#
# It does not repeat what that suite already proves about the limiter. It asks
# how far a Redis outage spreads: a feature that has nothing to do with rate
# limiting must stay completely available, or a defence-in-depth component has
# become a single point of failure. It stops and starts redis-server for real,
# so the shared-counter claim after recovery is made against a store that
# genuinely restarted.
tests/integration/dependency-failure-redis.spec.ts

# The dependency that fails here is somebody ELSE'S server: the customer's HTTP
# endpoint, which can be down for a week without this deployment being able to
# do anything about it. The contract is therefore the opposite of the others -
# keep the event, retry on a schedule, deliver exactly once on return - and the
# three ways that goes wrong (lost, duplicated, never) are each asserted.
#
# It also pins the distinction that makes the ladder work: the egress guard's
# refusal is TERMINAL, a connection refusal is not. Collapsing the two would
# either spam a forbidden URL or drop every event from a restarting receiver.
tests/integration/dependency-failure-webhook-receiver.spec.ts

# What happens when a migration FAILS halfway - the case an operator meets at
# 3am and the one where a wrong answer is unrecoverable.
#
# The rehearsal migration exists only in the assembled workspace, never in the
# repository, so a deliberately broken migration can never ship. It does real
# work and then fails inside one transaction, which is the RECOVERABLE shape
# and therefore the one worth proving first.
#
# It found that the failure was honest but ILLEGIBLE: execFileSync puts the
# reason on stderr and none of it in `message`, so an operator got
# "Command failed: <node> <cli> migrate deploy" while Prisma's P3018, the
# migration name, the SQL error and the recovery link were all discarded.
#
# The fixture installs the PostgREST support objects the way the installer
# does, from both SQL files in the installer's order. Without them case D is
# vacuous: "nothing was lost" is trivially true when there was nothing to lose.
tests/integration/selfhost-failed-migration.spec.ts

# ── Managed migration runner: ownership and failed-migration recovery ─────────
#
# The 2026-09-24 staging incident, rebuilt: a non-superuser admin builds the
# chain, the tables move to the app role, the enums stay behind, and the pause
# migration fails with 42501. Proves the ownership preflight refuses before
# Prisma writes history, rollback resolves only a genuinely absent failed
# attempt, and the enum repair converges and is idempotent. Real runner
# entrypoint, real Prisma CLI, real PostgreSQL. Needs CREATE DATABASE/ROLE.
tests/integration/migration-ownership-recovery.spec.ts

# ── Regional database initialisation ────────────────────────────────────────
#
# tools/managed-db/regional/bootstrap.sh, run from a copy of exactly the files
# its image carries, against a PostgreSQL 16 cluster the suite creates with
# initdb and throws away: the procedure creates cluster-wide roles by their real
# names, so it cannot share the service database. An administrator that is not
# a superuser, like the RDS master, then owns what was installed, and the
# application's own paths run against it. Needs PostgreSQL 16 server binaries
# (PG_BINDIR) and, in CI, pgvector; it fails rather than skips without them.
# It also pins the region's snapshots: a project the application makes there
# without direct access is dumped and restored by the real snapshot job as
# backenly_backup, and a workspace made before that fails pg_dump and verify.sql
# until the procedure is applied again. A check on its own fails on a step that
# changed and does not verify yet; only the check a launcher runs before its own
# apply (BOOTSTRAP_PRE_APPLY) reports it without failing. Mutation-checked: the
# previous code and SQL fail nine of those ten tests, with the exact "permission
# denied for schema" pg_dump error seen in us-east-1 (the tenth passes on the old
# verify.sql, which is the gap), and a check that tolerates every changed step
# fails the three that pin the strict check and the signal.
tests/integration/regional-bootstrap.spec.ts

# ── Credential rotation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# A rotation proven only by "the new password works" is not proven: the point of
# rotating is that the OLD credential STOPS working. Every case is control ->
# rotate -> old refused (28P01, not a timeout) -> new works -> security
# properties survived. The last step is the expensive one to skip: a rotation
# that recreated backenly_app as a superuser would pass the first four while
# turning every FORCE RLS policy into a suggestion.
#
# Roles are CLUSTER-WIDE, so this uses throwaway role names throughout - a
# separate database does not isolate them.
#
# It measures whether the cluster authenticates at all, with a password that is
# certainly wrong, and REFUSES to assert revocation on a `trust` cluster rather
# than reporting a false verdict. A developer's local PostgreSQL is usually
# trust; CI's postgres:16 is initialised with a password and scram-sha-256.
tests/integration/credential-rotation-database.spec.ts

# Rotating the secrets an operator types into the dashboard rather than into a
# connection string. It found that GET /api/workspace-oauth decrypted every
# provider's client secret and returned it to the browser, while the POST on the
# same endpoint redacted its own response - so the intent was never in doubt and
# the GET simply contradicted it.
tests/integration/credential-rotation-provider-secrets.spec.ts

# ── Scheduled snapshots ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# Default OFF, and it stays off: an upgrade must not start writing a dump of
# every project to disk nightly on somebody's behalf while they are not looking.
#
# Nothing here calls backupWorkspace directly - that is the point. The
# SCHEDULER'S own entry point is driven, including its auth gate, and the
# artifact it produces is opened and read for the marker row. Calling the backup
# function by hand proves the function works and says nothing about whether
# anything ever calls it.
#
# The failure case encodes a real production incident: nightly backups failed
# for four days while the pruner deleted the last good ones, ending at zero
# backups on disk with one info-level line as the only trace. So a failed run
# must leave a FAILED record and no artifact, never a completed record pointing
# at a file that is not there, and retention must protect a project whose latest
# run failed.
tests/integration/scheduled-snapshots.spec.ts

# HIGH, found by the final qualification on a real deployment: a PostgreSQL
# restart made the next /api/v1/* request reject with P1017 and the RUNTIME
# PROCESS EXITED. Express 4 does not await its handlers, so an async rejection
# never reaches the global error middleware - it becomes an unhandled rejection
# and Node 15+ terminates on those. Every v1 surface stayed down afterwards.
#
# The demonstration runs in a SUBPROCESS, because jest installs its own
# unhandledRejection handler and the thing under test - Node terminating - can
# never happen inside it. Wrapped: 500 and exit 0. Unwrapped: no response and a
# non-zero exit, which is the CI log exactly.
tests/integration/runtime-async-crash.spec.ts

# The fourth role. setup-app-role.ts and README.md have documented a four-role
# architecture since the credential split; three were created by code, and
# `backenly_backup` existed in prose plus a README section telling operators to
# run the CREATE ROLE by hand - with a grant list covering the workspace schema
# and NOT public, so even following it left recovery broken.
#
# Deployment Recovery therefore failed on every correctly split install with
# "permission denied for table backenly_pgrst_schema_registry". Every existing
# recovery test passed because they run where the role is a superuser.
#
# Granting the registry to the app role would have cleared that error and
# stopped at the next: workspace tables are FORCE RLS and backenly_app is
# NOBYPASSRLS. That is asserted here rather than argued - the app role is made
# to try both dumps, and fails both.
tests/integration/backup-role-contract.spec.ts

# only, so /db, /database, /v2, end-user sign-in, OAuth and realtime kept
# serving a locked project. The runtime serving gate now sits in front of all
# of them. This drives the REAL server/app.ts over a socket, because mount

tests/integration/runtime-serving-gate.spec.ts

# Governed changes and restoring them: every class of schema change (additive,

# Nothing outside a vault reads what is in it. A restore that would move aside a

# changed; a vault a live object still reads is kept past its window, never
# purged with CASCADE. Beside those: a reapply record cannot be restored, a

# Workspace SQL after a table's columns change. Prisma reused a prepared
# statement per pooled connection, and PostgreSQL refuses to run one whose
# result columns changed (0A000), so after an ALTER TABLE the v1 query and
# insert routes failed until the connection was replaced. Each case runs a
# statement, changes the table, and runs it again on the same client: the home
# and a regional client (a second database), executeWithUserContext, and a
# route-module function on its own login. What PostgreSQL refuses is the
# property, so it needs a real Postgres.
tests/integration/workspace-sql-cached-plan.spec.ts

# A home project's governed change records the statements it ran. Its
# workspace SQL runs on the home workspace client, not the platform client, so
# the SQL recorder has to be on that client too: a change runs its DDL through
# executeWithUserContext, and its record must carry that statement. The change
# ledger, its lock and its record are the property, so it needs a real Postgres.
tests/integration/home-workspace-sql-recorded.spec.ts

# A regional project's change record keeps structure at home and its
# definitions in its region: no function body, view query, CHECK, policy,
# default or generation expression, index or trigger statement, comment or
# enum label of a regional change, its restore or an interrupted one is on its
# home rows; the region keeps them under the change; a restore puts every
# definition back exactly from the region's copy, and refuses a copy altered or
# missing. A home project's record keeps its definitions as before. A second
# database stands in for the region, so it needs a real Postgres.
tests/integration/change-ledger-residency.spec.ts

# A project with a change history is deleted with the change ledger's guard
# installed as production has it: before the deletion the guard refuses
# deleting the changes or their events on their own; deleteProjectCompletely
# then removes the project, every change and event, the restore's vault and a
# preview branch, and leaves no schema in the project's namespace. The guard's
# triggers and the schemas are the property, so it needs a real Postgres.
tests/integration/project-deletion-change-ledger.spec.ts

# PostgREST forgets what a statement dropped or moved into a vault: with the
# real registry and DDL sync files installed in a database of their own, a
# DROP TABLE, DROP VIEW or DROP FUNCTION in a served schema and a move into
# that schema's vault each notify pgrst to reload its schema cache, nothing is
# granted in the vault, and DDL outside served schemas notifies nothing. Event
# triggers and notifications are the property, so it needs a real Postgres.
tests/integration/postgrest-reload-on-drop.spec.ts

# The SDK's filters mean the same on both servers that answer the data routes:
# isNull, isNotNull, eq, neq, gt and in on uuid, timestamp, integer and boolean
# columns, get, update and delete by a uuid id, an update or delete through
# isNull and in. A value its column cannot take answers 400 naming the column,
# a duplicate 409, and a filter neither can apply 400 with no row changed.
# What PostgreSQL accepts is the property, so it needs a real Postgres.
tests/integration/sdk-filters-both-servers.spec.ts
# The MCP data tools' filters (db_query, db_update, db_delete) build through the
# same builder: an invalid column name, an unknown operator, an operator object
# naming nothing or an $in that is not a list is refused with no row changed,
# where skipping it widened a service-role update or delete. What PostgreSQL
# matches is the property, so it needs a real Postgres.
tests/integration/mcp-filters-never-widen.spec.ts
# Where runBrain sends a turn, and every way its agent loop ends (#246): CONFIRM
# with nothing pending, the blueprint propose, execute and resume routes, a lost
# plan designed again, APPLY_PROPOSAL, no model configured, and the plain-text,
# needs-user, refused, rate-limited and timed-out exits. Run on the shared
# harness (tests/helpers/brain-harness.ts) with only the model scripted: the
# pending-plan store, conversation log and the tables a plan builds are real, so
# it needs a real Postgres.
tests/integration/brain-routing.spec.ts
# The brain's approval gate, run through the real loop for every tool it stops:
# each call is held exactly as issued, never run, and described on the card the
# approver reads (target, live row count, reversibility, the trigger or webhook
# it resolves), including a call repeated or issued beside a read. The rows
# counted and the trigger and webhook rows resolved are real, so it needs a real
# Postgres.
tests/integration/brain-approval-targets.spec.ts
# The blueprint turns of runBrain, whole: the proposal card for every kind of
# step, a plan's run (seeding, a step that throws, a destructive step it may not
# run, the resume queue), the post-build check's report in each of its outcomes,
# the requirements a person wrote reconciled against what was planned and built,
# and stored plans that are corrupt, expired or from before a field existed. The
# workspace tables a plan builds and the stored plans are real, so it needs a
# real Postgres.
tests/integration/brain-blueprint-turns.spec.ts
# The edges of a runBrain turn: what the classifier is told and how its answer is
# read, what each intent's loop is offered, every stop and the resume point it
# saves, billing of a call that ran before it failed, and what a turn writes down
# (conversation, receipts, a summary once the log is long). The conversation log,
# stored resume rows, receipts and workspace tables are real, so it needs a real
# Postgres.
tests/integration/brain-loop-edges.spec.ts

# The schema snapshot reads each kind of object once for the whole schema, so
# the number of queries it sends does not grow with the project's tables (a

# the table-by-table reader read. What PostgreSQL's catalog returns is the
# property, so it needs a real Postgres.
tests/integration/workspace-schema-snapshot-reader.spec.ts
